account:
This morning I read the original appointments and the signed addendum, then returned all four books. Today's business includes a ten o'clock grain inspection at the mill, council letters at thirteen hundred, tea with the neighbour at the east-bank cottage at fifteen hundred, office hours at sixteen thirty, and a great hall lighting inspection at eighteen hundred. The builder and secretary are to attend that inspection, which concerns eight installed lanterns and the lighting around four tables.

The unusual thing is the continuing uncertainty about the town accounts. The secretary has asked me for the ledger's identity, custodian and storage location, none of which I know. The builder and neighbour apparently do not know where the accounts are either; I heard the neighbour say that the baker also did not know. I asked the secretary to establish who last handled them rather than assume a cabinet or ledger. I have not received a finding. This is an unresolved records problem, not evidence that someone has stolen or concealed anything.

The innkeeper requested an eighteen hundred meeting about inn and town matters, conflicting with the approved inspection. I offered a meeting during morning office hours instead. He is here now with the secretary, builder and neighbour nearby, but I have not yet heard his business. My first invitation was heard only by the neighbour, so I moved closer. Several recent conversations were indistinct; I cannot claim to know their contents. Earlier I heard freight ask the innkeeper to discuss today's freight arrangements at the inn. That could simply be ordinary trade business.

There is a fair amount of contact among these people, but I do not yet know of a separate plan involving them. The confirmed purpose of the evening gathering is lighting inspection. I want to hear the innkeeper directly, learn any actual town news, and keep my scheduled appointments rather than infer a hidden purpose from conversations I could not understand.
